Thahash
THAY-hash
n. (a son of Nahor by his concubine Reumah, named once)
Hebrew Tachash, a badger, or the skin of some clean sea-creature used for the covering of the tabernacle; named once, Genesis 22:24.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Thahash is the third of the four sons borne to Nahor by his concubine: “And his concubine, whose name was Reumah, she bare also Tebah, and Gaham, and Thahash, and Maachah” (Genesis 22:24). The verse is the last of the chapter, and it is the shadow cast by the eight sons of Milcah named just above it. Scripture does not commend Nahor's arrangement; it records it, as it records the concubines of Abraham and of Jacob's sons, with the consequences left to the narrative. The Authorized Version uses the same word for the covering of the tabernacle: “a covering above of badgers' skins” (Exodus 26:14), and the name Thahash is that word. A man was called Badger, and the hide of that creature was afterward laid over the dwelling-place of God — the outermost, plainest layer, the one that took the weather. Of the man himself nothing further is written. He fathered no tribe the record follows, and his line is not traced. He belongs to the set of names Scripture preserves without comment: real, numbered, and silent. The line of promise ran through Milcah's eighth son, not through Reumah's third.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Thahash, a son of Nahor by his concubine Reumah, named once, Genesis 22:24; the name signifies a badger, or the skin used for the tabernacle covering.

Hebrew Tachash, a badger; also the skin of a clean sea-creature.

The same word names the outer covering of the tabernacle, Exodus 26:14.

It occurs once as a man's name in the Authorized Version, Genesis 22:24.

He is the third of four sons borne to Nahor by Reumah.

No descendant and no deed of his is recorded.

Key Scripture

Gen 22:24 — "And his concubine, whose name was Reumah, she bare also Tebah, and Gaham, and Thahash, and Maachah."

Gen 22:23 — "And Bethuel begat Rebekah: these eight Milcah did bear to Nahor, Abraham's brother."

Exo 26:14 — "And thou shalt make a covering for the tent of rams' skins dyed red, and a covering above of badgers' skins."

Num 4:25 — "And they shall bear the curtains of the tabernacle, and the tabernacle of the congregation, his covering, and the covering of the badgers' skins that is above upon it, and the hanging for the door of the tabernacle of the congregation,"

Modern Corruption

Concubinage in the patriarchal narratives is read as Scripture's endorsement; the text records the practice and lets its fruit be seen in whose line the promise did not run.

expand to see more

Two readings press on a verse like this one. The first is the progressive claim that because Scripture reports concubinage without a rebuke attached, Scripture approves it, and therefore biblical sexual ethics are negotiable. The second is the older liberal claim that such notices are tribal fiction. Both fail on the text. Genesis narrates Nahor's concubine in the same breath that it closes the account of Milcah's eight sons, and the chapter that follows traces Rebekah — Milcah's granddaughter. The record is not neutral about outcomes even where it is silent about verdicts. One-man-one-woman marriage is the creation ordinance of Genesis 2:24, and every departure from it in the patriarchal narratives yields grief, rivalry, or a line that goes nowhere.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that Scripture's silence is not consent. The Authorized Version names Reumah and her four sons, and never returns to them. A man may be truly recorded and still be outside the line of the covenant, and the way God kept His promise is read in whom He chose, not merely in whom He mentioned.
